title: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS WANT THE BLESSINGS OF ABRAHAM BUT AVOID THE OBEDIENCE OF ABRAHAM?
paragraphs: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS WANT THE BLESSINGS OF ABRAHAM BUT AVOID THE OBEDIENCE OF ABRAHAM?

We want Abraham’s promises, Abraham’s prosperity, and Abraham’s favor. But what happens when the same God who promises to bless us asks us to surrender the very thing we are afraid to lose? This is the uncomfortable truth about faith, obedience, and the blessing that money can never buy.
There is something deeply unsettling about the way we sometimes talk about Abraham.
We love the part where God promises to bless him.
We love the part where God promises to make his name great.
We love the part where God tells him that all the families of the earth will be blessed through him.
We quote those promises over our businesses, our finances, our children, our dreams, and our future.
But there is one part of Abraham’s story that doesn't appear nearly as often in our prayers.
The altar.
The knife.
The trembling hands of a father.
The son he had waited decades to hold.
And the voice of God asking him to surrender what he loved.
What if the greatest misunderstanding about Abraham's blessing is that we have been so busy asking God for what Abraham received that we have forgotten how Abraham responded?
And what if the real question isn't whether God wants to bless you?
What if the real question is whether you still trust Him when obedience threatens something you desperately want to keep?
Because the God who called Abraham is not merely the God who gives promises.
He is the God who calls people to trust Him enough to follow.
And that changes everything.
Genesis 12:1 records the beginning of Abraham’s extraordinary journey. God told Abram to leave his country, his kindred, and his father's house for a land that He would show him.
Notice something.
God did not begin by handing Abraham a complete map.
He began with a command.
Before Abraham saw the land, he had to leave home.
Before he became the father of a multitude, he had to walk away from what was familiar.
Before the fulfillment of the promise, there was a journey of faith.
And Hebrews 11:8 says that Abraham obeyed by faith, going out without knowing where he was going.
Think about that for a moment.
Abraham did not have the luxury of knowing how everything would turn out.
He had God's word.
And he went.
Some of us say we want Abraham's faith, but we will not take one step unless God first shows us the entire staircase.
We want confirmation without uncertainty.
We want provision without dependence.
We want an answer before surrender.
We want God to guarantee the outcome before we agree to obey.
But Abraham's journey confronts the comfortable version of Christianity that treats faith as a way of controlling the future.
Biblical faith is not controlling God.
It is trusting God.
And there is a difference.
The Hebrew language makes the beginning of Abraham's journey especially striking.
In Genesis 12:1, God's command includes the words לֶךְ־לְךָ (lekh-lekha).
The expression is commonly translated "Go" or "Go for yourself." The first word is an imperative from the Hebrew verb meaning to go or walk; the second is a form meaning "to you" or "for yourself."
It is sometimes given a devotional interpretation such as "go into yourself," but that is not its straightforward grammatical meaning in this passage.
The actual command is already powerful enough.
Leave.
Go.
Trust the One who is calling you.
Abraham's faith began with a real departure, not merely an inspiring feeling.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because you may not be called to leave your country.
But what about the relationship you know is drawing you away from Christ?
What about the dishonesty you have learned to excuse because it keeps your business profitable?
What about the bitterness you have carried so long that forgiveness feels like losing?
What about the private compromise that nobody in church knows about?
What about the habit you defend in public but secretly wish you could escape?
We can ask God to open doors while refusing to close the doors that lead us into sin.
We can pray for peace while clinging to resentment.
We can ask for a godly marriage while refusing to become a faithful, truthful, and loving person.
We can pray for financial blessing while treating generosity, honesty, and stewardship as optional.
And then we wonder why our spiritual lives feel divided.
Not every hardship is the result of disobedience. Scripture never gives us permission to accuse suffering believers of lacking faith.
But Scripture does call us to examine whether we are following the Lord we claim to trust.
And Abraham's story does not allow us to separate faith from its fruit.
James 2:22 says, in the King James Version, that Abraham's faith "wrought with his works, and by works was faith made perfect."
The Greek expression includes ἡ πίστις συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ (hē pistis synērgei tois ergois autou), meaning that faith was working together with his works.
James is not teaching that Abraham purchased salvation through religious performance.
He is showing that living faith becomes visible through action.
Paul makes equally clear in Romans 4:3 that Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness.
These truths are not enemies.
We are justified by God's grace through faith, not by earning salvation through good works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the grace that saves us also creates a new life in which good works have their proper place (Ephesians 2:10).
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase God's love. It is one of the fruits of a heart that has come to trust Him.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because if you believe obedience purchases God's acceptance, you will eventually become exhausted, proud, terrified, or hopeless.
But if you understand that Christ loved us while we were still sinners, obedience begins to take on a different meaning.
It becomes a response to grace.
Not a payment for grace.
And that brings us to the most terrifying chapter in Abraham's life.
Genesis 22.
Isaac was not merely Abraham's beloved son.
He was the child through whom God had specifically promised to continue His covenant purposes.
He represented years of waiting.
Years of disappointment.
Years of believing when circumstances appeared impossible.
And then came a test Abraham could never have imagined.
God commanded Abraham to offer Isaac.
Read that carefully.
Genesis 22 explicitly presents this as a test. It does not establish a general practice of human sacrifice, and the narrative ends with God preventing Isaac's death.
God's command to Abraham was extraordinary, not permission for anyone today to harm another person in the name of obedience.
But within that extraordinary event, Scripture reveals something profound about Abraham's trust.
Hebrews 11:17–19 explains that Abraham believed God was able even to raise the dead.
Abraham did not understand everything.
But he trusted the God who had made the promise.
Imagine walking up that mountain.
Imagine Isaac asking where the lamb was.
Imagine the weight of every step.
The son Abraham loved was walking beside him.
The promise Abraham had waited for was breathing beside him.
And yet Abraham believed that God's faithfulness was greater than what his eyes could understand.
Then, at the decisive moment, the angel of the LORD stopped him.
Isaac was spared.
And Abraham looked up and saw a ram caught in a thicket.
God provided the sacrifice.
Genesis 22:14 says Abraham named the place יְהוָה יִרְאֶה (YHWH yir'eh).
This is traditionally expressed as "The LORD will provide."
The Hebrew verb ra'ah ordinarily means "to see," and in this context the expression carries the sense of God's seeing to what is needed—His provision.
But notice what the passage does not promise.
It does not say that everyone who gives up something valuable will receive a larger bank account.
It does not say every painful act of obedience will produce an immediate earthly reward.
It does not say you can force God to multiply your possessions by making a dramatic sacrifice.
The story is about God's covenant faithfulness, Abraham's tested faith, and God's provision.
And its deepest significance becomes even clearer when we read it in the light of Jesus Christ.
Because on another day, centuries later, another beloved Son would walk toward sacrifice.
But this time, there would be no voice from heaven stopping the crucifixion.
No ram would take His place.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, would willingly give His life.
Isaac was spared.
Jesus was not spared from the cross.
And through His death and resurrection, sinners could receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
Romans 8:32 tells us that God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.
The Gospel is not ultimately about what we can sacrifice to persuade God to bless us.
It is about what God has done in Christ to rescue people who could never save themselves.
And this is where the message becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Abraham's obedience was remarkable.
But Abraham was not sinless.
He knew fear.
He made painful mistakes.
He lied about his relationship with Sarah in ways that endangered others.
He tried to navigate God's promise through human decisions that produced suffering and conflict.
His life was not a perfect record of spiritual victories.
It was a journey of faith in which a faithful God continued working through an imperfect man.
That should give hope to the believer who is reading this with tears in their eyes.
Maybe you have failed.
Maybe you knew what was right and still chose what was wrong.
Maybe you have made promises to God that you did not keep.
Maybe you have been living with the shame of a decision nobody else knows about.
You do not need to pretend that your failures were insignificant.
But you also do not need to believe they are stronger than the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Repentance is real.
Sin must not be romanticized.
Grace is not permission to continue in rebellion.
But the cross tells us that our failures do not have to be the final chapter of our lives.
And that is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by excusing sin.
But by forgiving, cleansing, restoring, and transforming sinners who come to Him in faith.
Now consider something else that is often overlooked.
When God promised to bless Abraham, the blessing was never meant to end with Abraham.
Genesis 12:3 declares that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him.
And Galatians 3:8 explains the significance of that promise in relation to the Gospel.
Paul goes even further in Galatians 3:16, identifying Christ as the ultimate promised offspring.
Then Galatians 3:29 declares that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise.
This is essential.
The blessing of Abraham cannot be faithfully reduced to wealth, property, status, or material comfort.
Yes, Abraham possessed substantial livestock, silver, and gold, as Genesis 13:2 records.
But his possessions were not the center of God's redemptive plan.
Christ was.

Galatians 3:13–14 explains that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and that we might receive the promised Spirit through faith.
The blessing is bound to the Gospel.
To belonging to Christ.
To the promised Spirit.
To God's saving purposes.
It is not a blank check promising every Christian the same earthly wealth Abraham possessed.
A faithful believer may be financially poor.
A devoted disciple may suffer persecution.
A generous Christian may endure unemployment, illness, or grief.
And none of those circumstances proves that God has abandoned them.
The apostles themselves endured hunger, hardship, imprisonment, and persecution.
Yet they were not outside the love of Christ.
So we must be careful when someone tells us that the blessing of Abraham guarantees prosperity if we simply perform the right spiritual transaction.
That is not what Paul teaches.
The greatest blessing of Abraham is not that you can become rich like Abraham. It is that, through Jesus Christ, you can belong to the God Abraham trusted.
And if we belong to Christ, then His words matter.
Jesus says in John 14:15, "If ye love me, keep my commandments."
The Greek text reads:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.
Ean agapate me, tas entolas tas emas tērēsete.
A faithful translation is, "If you love me, you will keep my commandments."
Notice the relationship.
Love and obedience belong together.
But Jesus is not inviting us into a loveless system of religious performance.
He is calling us into a relationship in which love expresses itself through faithfulness.
And the commandments of Christ include loving God, loving our neighbors, forgiving others, telling the truth, caring for those in need, making disciples, and denying ourselves to follow Him.
Sometimes obedience looks dramatic.
Sometimes it looks painfully ordinary.
It is the husband who chooses faithfulness when nobody is watching.
The wife who refuses to answer cruelty with cruelty.
The young person who walks away from temptation even though everyone else calls it normal.
The employee who tells the truth when a lie could bring promotion.
The believer who apologizes first.
The Christian who gives quietly without demanding recognition.
The wounded person who begins the difficult journey toward forgiveness without pretending that abuse was acceptable or abandoning necessary boundaries.
The disciple who chooses integrity even when integrity costs something.
No audience.
No applause.
No viral testimony.
Just a human heart saying, "Lord, I trust You."
And heaven is not impressed by the size of our public religious performance while our private lives are built on deliberate deception.
Jesus warned against practicing righteousness merely to be seen by others in Matthew 6.
He also warned in Matthew 7:21 that saying "Lord, Lord" is not the same as doing the Father's will.
Those are sobering words.
Because it is possible to know the vocabulary of faith while resisting the authority of Christ.
It is possible to sing about surrender while protecting the very thing God calls us to relinquish.
It is possible to celebrate Abraham's obedience in a sermon while refusing to obey Jesus in our homes.
And before we turn this message into a weapon against someone else, we should allow it to examine us first.
Not your neighbor.
Not your pastor.
Not the Christian who disappointed you.
You.
Me.
All of us.
Where are we asking God for blessings while resisting what His Word has already made clear?
Where have we confused God's patience with His approval?
Where have we mistaken outward success for spiritual maturity?
Where are we using the language of faith to hide an unwillingness to change?
These questions are uncomfortable.
But conviction can become a doorway to repentance.
The Holy Spirit does not need to flatter us into holiness.
He reveals truth and leads us toward Christ.
And the same Jesus who calls us to deny ourselves also invites the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest.
His yoke is not an invitation to earn salvation through endless religious anxiety.
It is an invitation to follow a Savior who is gentle and lowly in heart.
There is a reason the Gospel is good news.
It tells the truth about our sin.
And it tells an even greater truth about the mercy of God in Jesus Christ.
Perhaps you are reading this and realizing that you have been pursuing God's gifts more passionately than God's presence.
Perhaps your prayers have become a long list of things you want Him to do, while His Word has been calling you to something you keep avoiding.
Perhaps you have been waiting for a financial breakthrough when what you desperately need first is a restored relationship with Christ.
That does not mean your financial needs are unimportant.
Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread.
God cares about our needs.
But Jesus also said in Matthew 6:33 to seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness.
That is not a formula guaranteeing a luxurious life.
It is a call to place God's reign above our anxious pursuit of earthly security.
And maybe, today, the most important question you can ask is not, "Lord, when will You bless me?"
Maybe it is, "Lord, what have I been refusing to surrender?"
You might not receive an immediate answer to every problem.
Your circumstances might not change overnight.
Your obedience might cost you something.
But the Savior who calls you to follow Him has already demonstrated His love at Calvary.
You are not being asked to trust a stranger.
You are being invited to trust the One who gave Himself for you.
And if this message has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past that moment.
You do not need a public performance.
You need an honest response to God.
You can pray right where you are.

"Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have wanted Your gifts more than Your presence. Forgive me for calling You Lord while resisting Your Word. Search my heart. Expose what I have been hiding. Teach me to trust You when obedience is costly, when answers are delayed, and when I cannot see what comes next. Thank You for the cross, for Your mercy, and for the grace I could never earn. Help me follow You not to purchase Your love, but because You first loved me. Change my heart. Make my faith real. In Jesus' name, amen."
And if that prayer expresses what is happening inside you, I want to invite you into something more meaningful than simply reacting to another post.
You do not have to reveal private details.
Someone reading silently may need the encouragement that God has not abandoned them in their own struggle.
Your testimony does not have to be spectacular to be meaningful.
Sometimes the most powerful words are simply, "I was afraid, but Jesus helped me keep going."
And please, do not let this message stop with you.
Not because the algorithm measures your faith.
But because someone in your circle may be praying for blessings while quietly losing sight of the Savior.
Someone may be exhausted from believing that God only loves successful people.
Someone may be living in hidden compromise, desperately needing the courage to repent.
Someone may be one honest encounter with Scripture away from returning to Jesus Christ.
Not every post will be comfortable.
But our desire is that every message will lead you closer to Jesus Christ.
There is also a deeper invitation I want to place before you.
Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people grow in the Word of God, understand the Gospel, confront spiritual compromise, and discover the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
We want biblical nourishment to reach believers who cannot afford expensive resources.
We want struggling Christians to find encouragement grounded in Scripture.
We want seekers to encounter the truth of the Gospel.
We want families, young people, and believers in difficult seasons to have resources that point them back to Christ.
And this mission takes faithful work, time, resources, and the support of people who believe in it.
It is a practical way to participate in a ministry you value.
And there is an important biblical distinction worth making.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under pressure, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Jesus Christ is the Savior. Gospel Warrior is only a servant seeking to point people toward Him.
If you have the means, consider making Gospel Warrior part of your regular, prayerful generosity, alongside the responsibilities and ministries God has already placed on your heart.
These items are not spiritual rewards or signs of greater standing before God.
They are simply our way of expressing gratitude for those helping sustain the mission.
Keep reading.
Keep growing.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep following Jesus.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus paid the price we could never pay.
And that brings us back to Abraham.
To the man who left home without knowing the destination.
To the father who waited for a promise that seemed impossible.
To the believer whose faith was tested on a mountain.
To the imperfect servant whose life became part of a much greater story.
Abraham's ultimate significance was never merely the size of his possessions.
It was the faithfulness of the God who called him, sustained him, and fulfilled His redemptive promise through Jesus Christ.
And the same Gospel that points us to Abraham's promised offspring now calls us to repentance, faith, and a transformed life.
You may never own Abraham's wealth.
You may never experience his circumstances.
You may never be remembered by the world.
But through Jesus Christ, you can be reconciled to the God Abraham believed.
You can be forgiven.
You can be made new.
You can learn to obey, not as a frightened servant trying to purchase acceptance, but as a beloved child responding to grace.

And one day, when the applause fades, the possessions are gone, and every earthly achievement has lost its power to impress, what will matter is not how successfully we claimed the blessings of Abraham.
What will matter is whether we truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
So ask for daily bread.
Pray for provision.
Bring your dreams and burdens before the Father.
There is nothing wrong with asking God for good gifts.
But do not become so consumed with what is in His hands that you forget the Savior who gave Himself to bring you near.
And do not mistake the call to obedience for an invitation to save yourself.
Christ has already accomplished what sinners could never accomplish.
Now follow Him.
Trust Him.
When you fail, repent and return to Him.
When you are afraid, remember His faithfulness.
When obedience is costly, remember the cross.
When the future is uncertain, remember the empty tomb.
Because the greatest miracle in Abraham's story was never that a man became wealthy.
It was that the faithful God who made a promise would ultimately bring salvation to the nations through Jesus Christ.
You can spend your whole life reaching for Abraham's blessings and still miss the greatest blessing of all—the Savior Abraham's story was pointing toward.
